family_history: Mother had dementia, diagnosed in her late 70s (type unclear)

social_history.living_situation: Lives with daughter; son visits weekly

patient.chief_complaint: Progressive cognitive slowing and memory difficulties over 14 months, with subtle walking changes noticed by family over the past 6 months
patient.history_present_illness: A 76-year-old retired accountant was admitted for inpatient evaluation of progressive cognitive decline. Over the past 14 months, she has developed worsening 'brain fog,' slowed thinking, difficulty managing her household finances, and increasing trouble following complex conversations. Her daughter, a nurse, noted that her mother had become 'mentally slower' and less able to multitask — she previously balanced family accounts and organized community events independently but now requires help with both. The cognitive decline prompted her primary care physician to refer her to a geriatric psychiatrist, who diagnosed probable early Alzheimer's dementia two months ago based on her prominent cognitive symptoms, a family history of dementia (mother and sister), and a MoCA of 17/30 at that visit. No neuroimaging was obtained at that time. The family accepted this diagnosis and began researching memory care facilities. However, over the past 6 months her daughter has noticed a subtle change in her mother's walking — she now shuffles with small steps and seems to hesitate before stepping off curbs, and her feet appear to 'catch' on the carpet. There have been two near-falls. Additionally, she has developed urinary urgency with two episodes of incontinence over the past 4 months, which she attributes to 'being slow to the bathroom.' Her daughter brought her to the emergency department after reading about NPH online and requesting a second opinion on the Alzheimer's diagnosis. The patient herself is concerned about the cognitive changes and eager for evaluation; she denies tremor, sudden falls, visual hallucinations, or asymmetric limb symptoms.

neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert, oriented to person, place, and year but not month. MoCA 17/30 — primary deficits on delayed recall (2/5), executive tasks (clock drawing, trail-making analog, serial 7s), and attention. Naming intact (6/6 animals). Language fluent without aphasia. No visuospatial misperception. Processing speed markedly slowed on bedside tests.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Normal. No papilledema. Extraocular movements full, no nystagmus.
neurological_exam.motor: Normal tone. Full strength 5/5 throughout. No rigidity. No resting tremor.
neurological_exam.sensory: Mildly reduced vibration at ankles bilaterally. Light touch and proprioception intact.
neurological_exam.coordination: Finger-nose intact. Heel-shin mildly clumsy bilaterally.
neurological_exam.gait: Narrow-to-normal base but markedly shortened step length. Reduced foot clearance with low shuffling steps ('magnetic' quality). Initiation hesitation with start-stop on carpet crossing. TUG 28 seconds. 10-meter walk 22 seconds. No significant arm swing reduction. Pull test: 2 steps back, recovers. No festination. Gait does not resemble typical Parkinsonian gait (no pill-rolling tremor, no significant rigidity, symmetric).
neurological_exam.additional: Mild bilateral grasp reflex. Snout reflex positive. No nuchal rigidity. No evidence of cortical release signs beyond frontal grasp.

findings.location: bilateral lateral ventricles and third ventricle

signal_characteristics.description: Evans index 0.36 — above the diagnostic threshold of 0.30; moderate symmetric ventriculomegaly disproportionate to degree of cortical atrophy
Tight high-convexity sulci parasagittally with disproportionately widened Sylvian fissures — DESH morphology
Callosal angle 74 degrees on coronal T1 reformats — below the 90-degree threshold
Mild thinning of the corpus callosum body with upward bowing consistent with transventricular pressure effect
Smooth periventricular FLAIR caps and halos; Fazekas 2 periventricular, Fazekas 1 subcortical
Mild-to-moderate cortical atrophy, symmetric; hippocampal volumes appear mildly reduced but proportionate to age and global atrophy — not disproportionately atrophic
Prominent T2 aqueductal flow void, consistent with hyperdynamic CSF pulsatility

mri.impression: 1. Moderate ventriculomegaly; Evans index 0.36, disproportionate to degree of cortical atrophy. Callosal angle 74 degrees. DESH pattern — tight high-convexity sulci with widened Sylvian fissures. Mild corpus callosum thinning with upward bowing. Periventricular FLAIR signal (Fazekas 2). Prominent aqueductal flow void. 2. Mild-to-moderate symmetric cortical atrophy; hippocampal volumes mildly reduced, proportionate to global atrophy without focal mesial temporal predominance. No mass, hemorrhage, restricted diffusion, or obstructive lesion

labs.interpretation: All values within normal limits. Reversible metabolic and infectious causes of cognitive decline (hypothyroidism, B12 deficiency, neurosyphilis, HIV) not identified.

special_tests.urinary_urgency_post: Reduced — patient reported no urgency episodes in 24 hours post-tap

csf.interpretation: Opening pressure: 14 cmH2O (normal). WBC: 1 cell/mcL (lymphocyte). Protein: 44 mg/dL. Glucose: 64 mg/dL (ratio 0.67). Cytology: No malignant cells. High-volume tap trial (40 mL): TUG improved from 28 seconds pre-tap to 19 seconds at 24 hours (32% improvement); 10-meter walk improved from 22 seconds to 16 seconds at 24 hours (27% improvement); MoCA improved 3 points at 24 hours. Patient reported absence of urinary urgency episodes in the 24 hours post-tap

findings.result: Moderately-to-severely impaired — Trail Making Test Part B incomplete; COWAT phonemic 5 words/min (severely impaired); clock drawing with planning errors and perseveration
Severely impaired — WAIS-IV Coding age-corrected score 4 (0.2nd percentile); Symbol Search 5 (5th percentile)
Moderately impaired — Digit Span Forward 5 (25th percentile); Digit Span Backward 3 (5th percentile)

Mildly impaired — HVLT-R delayed recall 5/12 (12th percentile); recognition discriminability index within low-normal range (10th percentile); encoding and cued recall relatively preserved compared to free recall
Intact naming; mild word-finding pauses on confrontation naming (BNT 50/60). No aphasia.
Low-normal — Rey-Osterrieth Copy 28/36; constructional errors consistent with reduced planning rather than perceptual deficit

quantitative_data.overall_profile: Frontal-subcortical with severe executive and processing speed impairment disproportionate to episodic memory deficit; recognition memory relatively preserved

specialized_test.impression: Neuropsychological evaluation demonstrates severe executive dysfunction (COWAT, Trail Making B) and severely impaired processing speed disproportionate to episodic memory. Episodic memory is mildly impaired with relatively preserved recognition, distinguishing the profile from the cortical amnestic pattern typical of medial temporal Alzheimer-type impairment. Language intact. Profile is consistent with a subcortical-frontal cognitive pattern

scores.assessment timing: immediately before the large-volume tap, then repeated after it

pre_post_comparison.before the tap: Narrow-to-normal base but markedly shortened step length.; Reduced foot clearance with low shuffling steps ('magnetic' quality).; Pull test: 2 steps back, recovers.
pre_post_comparison.after the tap: TUG improvement >20% and 10-metre walk improvement >20% at 24 h; 10-metre walk improvement >20% at 24 hours; MoCA improvement ≥2 points — firmly positive tap tes

findings.result: Narrow-to-normal base but markedly shortened step length.
Reduced foot clearance with low shuffling steps ('magnetic' quality).

clinical_assessment.impression: Objective gait and balance measured before the large-volume tap and repeated after it, with the cognitive screen repeated alongside. The response reached the threshold accepted as positive, which is the single best predictor of shunt response and the reason this measurement, not the imaging, carries the therapeutic decision. Without a measured baseline the post-tap change cannot be interpreted, which is why this assessment precedes the puncture.

findings.result: Negative amyloid PET — CL score 8 (well below threshold of 24.4)

output.impression: Negative — sparse-to-no amyloid neuritic plaque density. CL score 8, well below the standard amyloid positivity threshold of 24.4 CL

output.query: iNPH cognitive-predominant presentation atypical NPH Alzheimer differential amyloid PET tap test

results.title: Cognitive-predominant presentations of iNPH: diagnostic challenges and outcomes
results.key_finding: A subset of iNPH patients present with cognitive slowing as the dominant symptom; gait disturbance may be subtle early and is under-weighed when cognitive decline is prominent. Amyloid PET negative result supports iNPH over Alzheimer's and predicts better cognitive shunt response.

results.title: Amyloid PET in NPH: prevalence of copathology and impact on shunt outcomes
results.key_finding: Approximately 50% of iNPH patients have amyloid PET positivity; amyloid-negative patients have significantly higher rates of cognitive improvement post-shunt (approximately 65-70%) compared to amyloid-positive patients (approximately 25-35%). Amyloid PET negativity supports favorable cognitive prognosis after VP shunting.

results.title: Tap test gait improvement thresholds and shunt response prediction — pooled analysis
results.key_finding: TUG improvement ≥20% and 10-meter walk improvement ≥20% at 24 hours are associated with VP shunt benefit in iNPH (PPV approximately 80-85% in pooled analysis). MoCA improvement ≥2 points at 24 hours post-tap is an additional favorable predictor.

output.summary: Published series indicate that a minority of iNPH patients present with cognitive slowing as the dominant symptom with subtle early gait; this atypical presentation carries risk of misdiagnosis as Alzheimer's dementia. A negative amyloid PET (CL score below 24.4) in the setting of iNPH-compatible imaging, Hakim triad features (including subtle gait), and a positive tap trial identifies patients likely to have favorable cognitive as well as gait outcomes after VP shunting. Approximately 50% of iNPH patients are amyloid PET positive; amyloid-negative patients have substantially higher rates of cognitive shunt benefit. Clinical correlation required for individual management decisions.

differential.key_features: Cognitive slowing plus family history of dementia created a compelling AD anchor, actively ruled out by negative amyloid PET and subcortical-frontal (not amnestic-cortical) neuropsychological profile

differential.diagnosis: Vascular cognitive impairment / subcortical ischaemic vascular disease
differential.key_features: Subcortical white matter changes and frontal-executive slowing overlap, but DESH with ventriculomegaly disproportionate to white matter burden and positive tap test favour iNPH
No visual hallucinations, REM sleep behaviour disorder, or marked fluctuations; symmetric motor findings without parkinsonism; DESH pattern and tap response not features of DLB

Executive dysfunction and frontal-subcortical pattern overlap, but no disinhibition, apathy-without-insight, or frontal predominant atrophy; ventriculomegaly with DESH and positive tap test not features of bvFTD

differential.diagnosis: Cerebral atrophy with secondary ex-vacuo ventriculomegaly
differential.key_features: Would require ventriculomegaly proportionate to sulcal atrophy and callosal angle >90°; MRI shows DESH with Evans 0.36 and callosal angle 74° disproportionate to mild-moderate atrophy, and tap response confirms pressure-responsive hydrocephalus

optimal_actions.action: Literature review of iNPH diagnostic criteria, cognitive-predominant presentations, and role of amyloid PET in distinguishing iNPH from Alzheimer's copathology
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Relkin 2005 INPH Study Group criteria; Tisell 2011 tap-test predictors; Williams 2016 review; data on cognitive-predominant iNPH and amyloid PET negativity as favourable prognostic marker

optimal_actions.action: Brain MRI — measure Evans index, callosal angle, assess DESH pattern; exclude mass effect, secondary hydrocephalus, and characterise degree of cortical atrophy vs. ventricular enlargement
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Evans index >0.3 (confirmed 0.36), DESH pattern (tight high-convexity + widened Sylvian sulci), callosal angle <90° (confirmed 74°), periventricular FLAIR signal; mild-moderate cortical atrophy without focal mesial temporal predominance; no mass effect

optimal_actions.action: Reversible-cause labs (TSH, B12, RPR, HIV) to exclude metabolic and infectious causes of cognitive decline before attributing syndrome to NPH
optimal_actions.expected_finding: TSH, B12, RPR, HIV all within normal range; reversible mimics excluded

optimal_actions.action: Baseline neuropsychological battery — characterise cognitive profile (subcortical-frontal vs. cortical-amnestic) and establish pre-tap reference for post-tap change measurement
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Subcortical-frontal pattern: severe executive dysfunction and processing speed impairment disproportionate to relatively preserved recognition memory; profile inconsistent with typical amnestic AD

optimal_actions.action: Large-volume lumbar puncture (30-50 mL tap test) with opening pressure and objective pre/post gait (TUG, 10-metre walk) and cognitive assessment
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Opening pressure <25 cmH2O; 40 mL CSF removed; TUG improvement >20% and 10-metre walk improvement >20% at 24 hours; MoCA improvement ≥2 points — firmly positive tap test

optimal_actions.action: Amyloid PET (recommended) — assess for AD copathology to inform shunt cognitive prognosis; load-bearing here because AD was the working diagnosis and negative result significantly shifts the differential and prognosis
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Negative amyloid PET (CL score below 24.4) — sparse-to-no amyloid plaque density; argues against significant AD copathology and supports favourable cognitive shunt outcome

optimal_actions.action: Measure gait and balance objectively before the large-volume tap — timed-up-and-go, 10-metre walk, step length, falls risk — and repeat the same measures and the cognitive screen after it. The baseline must be recorded before the puncture or the post-tap change cannot be interpreted
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Baseline timed gait recorded before the tap and repeated after it, with the response read against the >=20% threshold and the cognitive screen repeated alongside

optimal_actions.action: Neurosurgery consultation for VP shunt candidacy after imaging, tap test, and amyloid PET are complete
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Neurosurgery accepts patient for VP shunt with programmable valve; goals-of-care discussion regarding gait, fall prevention, and cognitive recovery prognosis informed by negative amyloid PET

useless_tools.rationale: EEG is non-specific for NPH and does not contribute to differentiating iNPH from Alzheimer's dementia or other neurodegenerative causes in this chronic cognitive-gait presentation
ECG is unrelated to the NPH diagnostic workup; syncope or palpitations are not part of this presentation
Echocardiography does not contribute to NPH evaluation; no cardioembolic or syncope indication in this presentation
Head CT is inferior to MRI for Evans index measurement, callosal angle, and DESH assessment; only justified if MRI is contraindicated
Cardiac monitoring has no diagnostic role in this presentation of chronic cognitive slowing and gait difficulty without syncope or arrhythmia symptoms

sequence_constraints.reason: MRI must precede large-volume LP to exclude mass effect or secondary obstructive hydrocephalus before removing 30-50 mL of CSF
The baseline gait and cognition must be measured before the large-volume tap, or the post-tap change cannot be interpreted and the tap test yields nothing

critical_actions: Do not close the diagnosis as Alzheimer's dementia on the basis of cognitive symptoms alone when the gait examination demonstrates a magnetic quality and the MRI shows ventriculomegaly with DESH
Obtain brain MRI before lumbar puncture to exclude mass effect or obstructive hydrocephalus
Quantify gait with TUG and 10-metre walk before the tap test to enable objective pre/post comparison
Remove 30-50 mL of CSF during the tap test (under-sampling biases toward false-negative result)
Re-assess gait and cognition 1-4 hours after the tap and at 24 hours to capture the full response window

Order amyloid PET to assess for AD copathology — a negative result in the context of DESH + magnetic gait + positive tap reframes the diagnosis to shunt-responsive iNPH with favourable cognitive prognosis
Refer to neurosurgery for VP shunt evaluation once imaging, tap test, and amyloid PET are complete
contraindicated_actions: Do not diagnose Alzheimer's dementia and forgo NPH workup when ventriculomegaly with DESH and a magnetic gait disturbance are present — these features mandate iNPH evaluation regardless of cognitive symptom predominance
Do not perform large-volume lumbar puncture before MRI excludes mass effect or obstructive hydrocephalus

Do not interpret the neuropsychological profile as typical AD without noting the disproportionate executive and processing-speed impairment with relatively preserved recognition memory — this subcortical-frontal pattern is atypical for medial temporal Alzheimer's disease
Do not rely on family history of dementia as sufficient to anchor a diagnosis of Alzheimer's disease in the presence of unaddressed hydrocephalus imaging findings
key_reasoning_points: Cognitive-predominant iNPH is an atypical but recognised presentation in which executive slowing and processing-speed impairment dominate over gait; the gait disturbance is subtle early and easily under-weighted — scrutiny of gait quality (magnetic quality, initiation hesitation, reduced foot clearance) is essential even when it is not the chief complaint

The neuropsychological profile in iNPH is subcortical-frontal: severe executive dysfunction and processing speed impairment with relatively preserved recognition memory; this pattern is distinct from the cortical amnestic profile of medial temporal Alzheimer's disease where free and cued recall fail in parallel

A negative amyloid PET (CL score below 24.4) in a patient with iNPH-compatible imaging, Hakim triad features, and a positive tap test argues strongly against significant AD copathology and supports a favourable cognitive prognosis after VP shunting — approximately 65-70% cognitive improvement vs. 25-35% in amyloid-positive patients

Family history of dementia and prominent cognitive symptoms are anchor-producing features that can suppress recognition of the subtle magnetic gait and urinary urgency; the full Hakim triad must be sought systematically in all patients with new ventriculomegaly on imaging

Evans index >0.3 with DESH (tight high-convexity sulci + widened Sylvian fissures) and callosal angle <90° on MRI constitute the imaging diagnosis of probable iNPH; the callosal angle of 74° and DESH in this patient are clear — this is not borderline imaging

A positive tap test (TUG improvement ≥20% at 24 hours) combined with normal CSF opening pressure (<25 cmH2O) and negative amyloid PET provides high positive predictive value for durable VP shunt benefit in both gait and cognition
Tier per the July 2026 clinical review: The reversible-cause screen is good practice but does not establish or exclude hydrocephalus; the tap test does.

red_herrings.data_point: Prior diagnosis of probable early Alzheimer's dementia by geriatric psychiatry two months before admission, based on cognitive symptoms and family history
red_herrings.intended_effect: All cognitive and motor symptoms are attributed to Alzheimer's disease progression; the ventriculomegaly, DESH, and subtle magnetic gait are ignored or attributed to cerebral atrophy, foreclosing NPH evaluation
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: The AD diagnosis was made without neuroimaging and without examining gait quality; brain MRI showing Evans 0.36 with DESH and callosal angle 74° mandates iNPH evaluation, and the negative amyloid PET further argues against AD as the primary diagnosis

red_herrings.data_point: Family history of dementia in mother and sister — loaded anchor toward hereditary Alzheimer's disease
red_herrings.intended_effect: Family history of dementia increases Bayesian prior for Alzheimer's disease and reinforces premature diagnostic closure, leading the clinician away from considering a treatable hydrocephalus syndrome
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Family history of dementia is a risk factor but not a diagnosis; the imaging findings (DESH, Evans 0.36, callosal angle 74°), neuropsychological subcortical-frontal profile, and positive tap test are more diagnostically specific than family history alone

metadata.difficulty_variant_description: Diagnostic-puzzle iNPH in a 76-year-old woman with a cognitive-predominant atypical presentation and a prior Alzheimer's diagnosis as the primary red herring. Subtle magnetic gait under-weighted. Negative amyloid PET is the load-bearing mirror image of NPH-P01 (amyloid-positive copathology). Firmly positive tap test and clear DESH/callosal angle imaging confirm shunt-responsive iNPH.
metadata.revision_reason: July 2026 clinical tool review: the comment asks that advanced imaging be removed from NPH. Kept as optional in every case because all 30 use amyloid or FDG PET for the Alzheimer differential rather than as a test for NPH; this case was the last one left at recommended, so the tier is now uniform and the claim made to the reviewers is exact
metadata.difficulty_rationale: 7 optimal actions including 5 required tools (MRI, labs, neuropsych battery, large-volume tap, neurosurgery consult) plus 2 recommended (literature search, amyloid PET); 2 grounded red herrings (prior AD diagnosis, family history of dementia); differential includes AD as primary alternative that must be actively ruled out; cognitive-predominant atypical presentation suppresses recognition of subtle gait; negative amyloid PET is load-bearing and distinct from all other NPH cases in v5 set that are either amyloid-positive (P01) or do not use PET as a diagnostic pivot
